preamble: An election puzzle: 12 solutions contain a word from a group, not further defined in their clues.

clue.text: Journalist cuts article and stories from Italy

indicators.note: something that cuts into a thing pushes in between its parts, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: the definite article
short for editor, the usual crossword journalist
the unclued theme prime minister, David Cameron, supplied by the preamble

explanation.surface: A reporter trims a piece of writing along with some news stories filed from Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: Twelve answers here contain a British prime minister who gets no wordplay at all, as the preamble warns; this clue builds only the first five letters and David Cameron is simply added.
explanation.definitionFit: Boccaccio's Decameron is a fourteenth-century collection of a hundred tales told by Florentines escaping the plague.

clue.text: Land's politician admitting slip before Congress

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so the outer piece takes the others inside it

parts.note: a Tory is a British Conservative politician
to slip is to make a mistake
IT is crossword slang for sex, and congress can mean sexual intercourse

explanation.surface: A politician concedes a blunder before appearing in front of the US Congress.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital C dresses the last word up as the American legislature, but it is sexual congress; 'before' only orders the two pieces that go inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A territory is an area of ground under one government's control, so the two nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Country's leader going to display sloth, say

indicators.note: when the leader goes, the front letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: a country is a state; without its first letter it becomes this

explanation.surface: A national leader goes off to show how lazy they can be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country's leader' reads as a head of government, which suits the theme, but it is the first letter of STATE that goes; Anthony Eden, PM 1955-57, comes first unclued.
explanation.definitionFit: Edentates are an old order of toothless mammals including sloths, anteaters and armadillos, so a sloth is one example.

clue.text: Displays awkward pose capturing vote

indicators.note: to capture is to take and hold, so one piece is held inside the other
something awkward is clumsy and out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a cross on a ballot paper marks a vote

explanation.surface: Someone strikes an uncomfortable stance while casting a ballot, perhaps for a photographer.
explanation.walkthrough: X for a vote comes from marking a cross on the ballot paper, apt in an election puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Expos are exhibitions or trade shows, large public displays of goods or work.

clue.text: Sign that a group's forgotten tango dancing

indicators.note: dancers move about, so the remaining letters change places
something forgotten is left out, so a letter is removed

parts.note: taken as written
tango is T in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A notice says a dance group has dropped the tango from its repertoire.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'has': a group has forgotten tango, so one of the two Ts in the fodder goes before the rest is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To sign something is to write your signature on it, which is what an autograph is, as both noun and verb.

clue.text: English city, spot where head of state dwells

parts.note: Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire
to spot something is to see it

explanation.surface: A guide to an English city points out the spot where the monarch lives.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an English royal residence, but the head of state is the French president.
explanation.definitionFit: The Élysée Palace in Paris is the official residence of the President of France.

clue.text: Statesman, something of an egomaniac

indicators.note: 'something of' means a part of, so only a stretch of the following letters is used

parts.note: the run of letters in the middle of this word

explanation.surface: A comment that a certain politician is a bit of an egomaniac.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Statesman' is read literally as a man of a state, here a citizen of the Gulf state of Oman, not a senior politician.
explanation.definitionFit: Read cryptically, a statesman is any man belonging to a state, and a native of Oman fits.

clue.text: South Wimbledon and the like?

parts.note: the unclued theme prime minister, John Major, supplied by the preamble
the compass abbreviation

explanation.surface: A note that the London district of South Wimbledon is one of several similar places.
explanation.walkthrough: South Wimbledon looks like the London district and Tube station; in fact the S just follows the unclued theme leader John Major, PM 1990-97.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis the four Grand Slam tournaments, Wimbledon among them, are called the majors.

clue.text: Leader, a swine defended by right-wing tabloid

indicators.note: whatever is defended is surrounded by its protector, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: the Sun is a right-leaning British tabloid newspaper
a hog is a pig

explanation.surface: A tabloid newspaper sticks up for a politician everyone else thinks is a pig.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British daily tabloid that has long backed the Conservatives.
explanation.definitionFit: A shogun was the hereditary military ruler of feudal Japan, so a leader in the historical sense.

clue.text: Admit a lot of vice

indicators.note: a lot of something is most but not all of it, so the end is lost

parts.note: taken as written
greed is one of the seven deadly sins, a vice, cut short here

explanation.surface: A confession of having plenty of bad habits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lot of' reads as one phrase meaning much, but the A is kept as a letter and 'lot of' trims the vice.
explanation.definitionFit: To admit a point in argument is to concede or accept it, which is one sense of agree.

clue.text: Cent remains in fund for incidental expenses

parts.note: the unclued theme prime minister, William Petty, Earl of Shelburne, supplied by the preamble
the usual abbreviation for cent
ash is what remains after burning

explanation.surface: Every last cent left over goes into the office kitty.
explanation.walkthrough: The unclued opening is the theme leader: the Earl of Shelburne, PM 1782-83, was born William Petty.
explanation.definitionFit: Petty cash is a small sum kept on hand in an office to pay for minor day-to-day purchases.

clue.text: Narcotics, one ingested by Roundheads?

indicators.note: what is ingested ends up inside the eater, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: split as round, a ring shape, plus heads, which are pates
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Parliamentarian soldiers of the English Civil War taking drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: Roundheads were Cromwell's Parliamentarian troops, named for their cropped hair; here the word splits into round and heads, and only the heads take in the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Opiates are drugs derived from opium, such as morphine, and narcotics is the general term for them.

clue.text: Popular government's leader is showing age

parts.note: the unclued theme prime minister, Earl Grey, supplied by the preamble
something popular is in fashion

indicators.note: a leader comes first, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of this word

explanation.surface: A well-liked prime minister is starting to look old in office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Government's leader' sounds like a prime minister, but it supplies only a letter; the real one, Earl Grey of the 1832 Reform Act, opens the answer unclued.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair turning grey is the classic visible sign of getting older, so greying means showing your years.

clue.text: Wear a boring Briton's garment

parts.note: to sport clothes is to wear them

indicators.note: a drill boring into something goes inside it

parts.note: a Scot is a Briton from Scotland
taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to put on the clothes of a dull Briton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' looks like dull, describing the Briton, but it signals one piece drilling into another.
explanation.definitionFit: A sports coat is a man's casual tailored jacket, one kind of garment.

clue.text: Awful career, not a person heading for the top

indicators.note: something awful is in a dreadful state, so the letters are thrown into disorder
'not' says the following letter is left out

parts.note: taken as written
the letter removed

explanation.surface: A dreadful job, and not one for someone ambitious to get ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: The unclued theme leader is Lord Melbourne, whose family name was Lamb; it sits inside the rearranged letters of the job.
explanation.definitionFit: A clamberer scrambles upwards using hands and feet, so it is someone climbing towards a summit.

clue.text: Jailed Liberal group?

parts.note: to be jailed is to be in the can, slang for prison, so this word both supplies the outside and puts the other piece in it
the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A question about whether a band of Liberal politicians has been locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The can' is slang for prison, so 'jailed' means in the can and gives both the outer letters and the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A clan is a family group or a close-knit set of people with shared interests.

clue.text: Many to quit country after day for poor counsel

indicators.note: when these letters quit, they leave the word, and what is left is used

parts.note: the abbreviation for Monday
Germany with its last four letters gone

explanation.surface: Bad advice telling crowds of people to leave the country the day after something happens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Many' reads as a crowd, but it is the letters that quit a European country. Andrew Bonar Law, PM 1922-23, is the unclued theme opening.
explanation.definitionFit: A lawmonger is a contemptuous term for a low or pettifogging lawyer, so a counsel of poor quality.

clue.text: Wobbly tum bared to reveal tattoo

indicators.note: something wobbly shakes about, so the letters move out of place

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone lifts their shirt to show off a tattoo on a flabby belly.
explanation.walkthrough: Tattoo is not the inked picture the surface suggests but its other meaning, a military drum signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A tattoo was originally a drum or bugle signal recalling soldiers to quarters, hence a rhythmic beat on a drum.

clue.text: Uncovered soy sauce

parts.note: the unclued theme prime minister, Theresa May, supplied by the preamble

indicators.note: with its covering stripped off, the outer letters go and only the inside remains

parts.note: the letter at the heart of this word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Soy sauce' looks like one item, but only the middle of the first word is used and the second is the definition; Theresa May, PM 2016-19, is unclued.
explanation.definitionFit: Mayo is the everyday short form of mayonnaise, a cold sauce of egg yolk and oil.

clue.text: Plan working out capital for Africans

parts.note: to map something out is to plan it

indicators.note: something being worked is being shaped and kneaded, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A scheme being drawn up to raise money for African people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working out' looks like a single phrase meaning devising, but the first word rearranges the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Maputo is the capital city of Mozambique, a country in south-east Africa.

clue.text: Fried food is a pig's ear — and then seconds!

parts.note: a pig's ear is British slang for a botched job, just as a hash is
the unclued theme prime minister, Gordon Brown, supplied by the preamble
the abbreviation for seconds

explanation.surface: A diner says the fry-up was a mess, yet goes back for a second helping.
explanation.walkthrough: To make a pig's ear of something, in British slang, is to make a mess of it. Gordon Brown, PM 2007-10, sits unclued in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Hash browns are patties of grated potato fried until crisp, a breakfast side dish.

clue.text: Lead in shoplifting case

indicators.note: the lead is what comes first, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of this word
the unclued theme prime minister, Edward Heath, supplied by the preamble

explanation.surface: A detective heads up the investigation into a theft from a shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' is the definition, not a court matter, and 'lead in' takes one letter; Edward Heath, PM 1970-74, follows it unclued.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheath is a close-fitting cover, such as the scabbard for a blade, so a protective case.

clue.text: Exercise fan consuming a snack

indicators.note: whatever consumes something takes it inside, so the pair before this word hold the next piece

parts.note: physical education, school exercise
an enthusiast, as in a fitness nut
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fitness enthusiast eats something between workouts.
explanation.walkthrough: It is the two pieces together, side by side, that swallow the single letter between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Peanuts are eaten as a salted snack with drinks, so one is a nibble between meals.

clue.text: Saw media manipulation across Britain

parts.note: public relations, the business of managing coverage
across and over both mean from one side to the other
the abbreviation for Britain

explanation.surface: Someone witnessed spin doctoring going on throughout the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like the past tense of see, but it is the noun for an old saying.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is an old saying or maxim, the same thing as a familiar proverb.

clue.text: Round openings with no actual fit, regularly

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: Round holes into which nothing quite fits properly.
explanation.walkthrough: Start from the second letter of 'no' and take every other letter through to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: An oculus is a circular window or an opening at the top of a dome; the plural uses the Latin form.

clue.text: VIP discussed problem about English

indicators.note: what is discussed is spoken, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: a sum is an arithmetic problem
on as in a talk on a subject, meaning concerning
the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: An important person talked through a difficulty concerning England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a reversal or container signal but simply means on, concerning.
explanation.definitionFit: To be a someone is to be a person of importance, the informal opposite of a nobody.

clue.text: WC has to be fixed and sound

indicators.note: something to be fixed must be repaired and put back together differently

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A plumber's verdict that the toilet needs repairing but otherwise works fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like an adjective meaning in good order, pairing with 'fixed', but it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A schwa is the neutral unstressed vowel sound, as at the start of 'about', written as an upside-down e.

clue.text: Direction to Pole back in quiet street abroad

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only the final letter is taken

parts.note: the final letter of this word
rue is French for street
the unclued theme prime minister, Lord North, supplied by the preamble

explanation.surface: Directions given to a Polish visitor heading back to a quiet street overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' looks like a Polish person but is the geographic pole. 'Quiet' wants to be P or SH, but only its last letter counts; Lord North, PM 1770-82, is unclued.
explanation.definitionFit: True north is the direction towards the geographic North Pole, as opposed to magnetic north.

clue.text: Figure scoffed loudly

indicators.note: said loudly means spoken out, so the sound of the word counts

parts.note: to scoff food is to eat it greedily

explanation.surface: Someone sneered at a number, jeering out loud.
explanation.walkthrough: Scoffed reads as mocked, but in British slang to scoff is to wolf down food.
explanation.definitionFit: Eight is a number, and a figure is a numeral or number.

clue.text: Drops sound of glib talk after ruler

parts.note: the unclued theme prime minister, Pitt the Elder or Younger, supplied by the preamble
Elizabeth Regina, the Queen
patter is smooth, practised talk, like a salesman's

explanation.surface: A monarch gives up on the smooth talk of the courtier who comes after them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drops' looks like a verb meaning gives up, but it is the noun, raindrops. The unclued opening is Pitt, Elder or Younger, both prime ministers.
explanation.definitionFit: Pitter-patter imitates the light rapid tapping of rain or footsteps, the noise falling drops make.
